nodes.description: Homozygous germline GIPC3 variants in consanguineous families. The reported spectrum is mostly missense, spread across the N-terminal GH1 region, the PDZ domain and the C-terminal GH2 region, together with a frameshift (c.685dupG), a nonsense variant (c.903G>A, p.Trp301*) and a canonical splice-site variant (c.226-1G>T) that causes use of an alternative acceptor, a frameshift and a premature stop codon. The truncating alleles make loss of function the most direct reading of the missense alleles too, but no study has measured the activity of a patient missense protein.

nodes.description: The standard intervention for severe-to-profound sensorineural loss. One GIPC3 patient (DFNB95, individual II.1) is reported to have been implanted after an audiogram at 11.5 years of age, following progression to profound loss; no outcome is reported. The spiral ganglion degeneration seen in aged ahl5 mice is a theoretical concern for implant benefit, but has not been looked for in patients.

nodes.description: In Gipc3 knockout inner hair cells the cuticular plate fails to flatten and to take its normal rounded-rectangular shape, and junctions between inner hair cells and adjacent inner phalangeal cells are severely disrupted. How this produces the profound deafness of the knockout is not shown; it is left without a downstream edge rather than wired to the hearing-loss phenotype on inference.

nodes.description: Around postnatal day 12, control inner hair cells acquire a large, rapidly activating potassium current; ahl5 inner hair cells keep the small currents typical of postnatal day 6. The authors link the immature currents to the enlarged ABR wave I amplitude and audiogenic seizure susceptibility of young ahl5 mice, which have no reported human counterpart. No source connects this defect to the human hearing loss, so the node has no downstream edge.

meta.association: Biallelic pathogenic variants in GIPC3 cause DFNB15/DFNB72/DFNB95. GIPC3 was first implicated in two small families (Indian DFNB15, Dutch DFNB95) alongside the ahl5 mouse, and statistically significant linkage came from six large Pakistani DFNB72 families. An adjacent 19p locus, DFNB81, is genetically distinct and not caused by GIPC3. Across populations GIPC3 is a rare cause of recessive deafness, with one exception: a founder missense allele, c.245A>G (p.Asn82Ser), in the Chuvash population of Russia.

nodes.description: A naturally occurring PDZ-domain missense allele underlying the ahl5 hearing-loss locus and the jams1 audiogenic-seizure locus. Mice have moderate hearing impairment at 4 weeks that becomes profound by one year, disorganised stereocilia bundles, reduced transduction currents, immature inner hair cell potassium currents, and late degeneration of the organ of Corti and spiral ganglion. Transgenic wild-type Gipc3 restores hearing thresholds at the click, 8 kHz and 16 kHz stimuli. The juvenile audiogenic seizures have no counterpart reported in patients.

The IMPC global knockout, closer in kind to the truncating patient alleles. It is profoundly deaf by one month, with malformed cuticular plates, compressed hair bundles and disrupted inner hair cell junctions, but largely normal early transduction currents.

In ahl5 mice the organ of Corti and spiral ganglion are histologically normal at 8 weeks, but by 52 weeks the organ of Corti has degenerated from base towards apex and the spiral ganglion has lost many neurons, in parallel with progression of the hearing loss from high to low frequencies. Whether the same degeneration occurs in patients, most of whom have early non-progressive loss, is unknown.

nodes.description: GIPC3 is expressed in cochlear inner and outer hair cells and spiral ganglion neurons. In hair cells it starts out cytoplasmic and becomes concentrated in the cuticular plate and at apical cell junctions during postnatal development. It binds myosin VI (MYO6) directly, depends on MYO6 for its junctional localisation, and binds PDZ-binding motifs of cytoskeletal and junctional proteins including MYO18A. The proposed role is as an adaptor coupling MYO6 to the actin structures of the hair cell apex; the older hypothesis, from its punctate cytoplasmic staining, was a role in vesicle trafficking. All of this is mouse and chicken data.
